newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Karadzic plays "evil" role in Bosnia -- Bildt.
newsitem.headline: Karadzic plays "evil" role in Bosnia -- Bildt.

text.p: An international envoy's spokesman said on Thursday that Radovan Karadzic was a "force of evil" in Bosnia and still exerted strong influence in Serb territory despite promises to stay out of politics.

Karadzic, the former Bosnian Serb president indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, "seeks consistently to influence the political process," said Colum Murphy, spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt.

"He remains a force of evil and intrigue which can only taint those personalities and those institutions of (the Serb republic) which continue to tolerate his activities," Murphy told a news conference.
Karadzic agreed under international pressure to step down as Bosnian Serb president last year after leading Serb separatists during Bosnia's 1992-95 war.
In a report to the U.N. Security Council, Bildt called on the international community to limit its contacts with another Serb leader, Momcilo Krajisnik, because of his ties to Karadzic.

He recommended that international contacts with Krajisnik, the Serb member of the peacetime collective presidency, be "limited to essential business related to his function as a member of the presidency."

Intelligence reports and "chauvinistic policies" in Bosnia's Serb republic showed Karadzic still had his hands on the reins of power from his offices in Pale, 16 km (10 miles) outside Sarajevo, he said.
Murphy said: "There is a close link between Mr Krajisnik and Mr Karadzic which we believe to be irrefutable."
Bildt's report coincided with a power struggle in Serb territory between Krajisnik and Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic.

Krajisnik and other officials loyal to Karadzic have moved to isolate Plavsic after she tried to expose a wartime smuggling ring and criticised attempts to patch up relations with their patrons in Serbia.
Diplomats, who asked not to be named, that Western envoys would consult Plavsic more often in future to show their dissatisfaction with Krajisnik.
Murphy accused Krajisnik of allowing Serb media to refer to him incorrectly as the "president of the Serb republic" and of issuing misleading statements about the peace treaty.
"I think he (Krajisnik) will know that the international community is not to be fooled by juggling with titles and juggling with the syntax of the peace agreement," he said.

Bildt's report, which reviewed efforts to implement the Bosnian peace agreement, said its political success would be jeopardised if indicted war criminals were allowed to hold public office or exert authority.
Three suspects indicted by the war crimes tribunal hold public office in two towns in Serb territory and Croat suspects live openly in the central town of Vitez, Murphy said.
Bildt also called on international organisations to cease contacts with the Serb municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Foca except for arranging elections or for humanitarian reasons.
